subsection: 1. Origins of the Cold War, the division of Germany and the Sovietisation of Eastern Europe, 1945–1949

notes.h: Background: the Grand Alliance and the ideological divide
notes.b: The Cold War grew out of a wartime partnership that was always uneasy. The USA, Britain and the Soviet Union were allies against Hitler, but they stood for opposite systems and never fully trusted one another.
points: The Grand Alliance began in 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June and the USA entered the war in December. The allies fought together because they shared an enemy, not because they shared aims.

Distrust was old. The West had intervened against the Bolsheviks after 1917, and Stalin had signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact with Hitler in August 1939, so each side suspected the other of putting its own interests first.
Capitalism means private ownership and production for profit in a market economy; it was the system the USA defended. Western democracy added free elections and several parties competing for power.

Communism, as practised in the Soviet bloc (the group of states under Soviet leadership), meant a single party controlling the state, with industry publicly owned and centrally planned. The two systems each claimed to be the future, which made lasting friendship unlikely.

Soviet war dead numbered over 20 million (estimates go up to about 27 million), and Germany had invaded Russia through Poland in 1914 and again in 1941. This is why Stalin demanded security on his western frontier.

The Cold War is the rivalry of the two blocs short of direct war between the superpowers (the USA and the Soviet Union). It was fought by propaganda, aid, alliances, arms and crises, and is dated about 1945 to 1991.
The term was used by the American financier Bernard Baruch in a 1947 speech and popularised by the journalist Walter Lippmann's book The Cold War (1947).
notes.tip: A source question on Soviet security wants you to pick out why Stalin wanted friendly governments, such as invasion routes through Poland and Romania and huge war losses, and link that to the buffer zone.

notes.h: Wartime tensions, 1941–1944
notes.b: Even while Germany was still undefeated, quarrels over strategy and over Poland showed that the allies wanted different things from the peace. These disputes shaped the bargaining at Yalta.
points: The second front argument: Stalin pressed the Western allies to open a second front in western Europe to relieve the Red Army, and resented the delay because the Soviet Union was bearing the brunt of the fighting.

Katyn: Polish officers had been murdered by the Soviet NKVD (secret police) in 1940. In 1943 the Polish government-in-exile in London asked for an inquiry, so the Soviet Union broke off relations with it.

The Warsaw Rising of August–October 1944 was a Polish revolt against the Germans. The Red Army did not come to its aid, which Poles and the West read as Stalin letting non-communist resistance be crushed.

In October 1944 in Moscow, Churchill and Stalin informally agreed spheres of influence (areas where one power's wishes would prevail) in the Balkans. This percentages agreement was an informal note, not a formal treaty.

The percentages gave the Soviet Union predominance in Romania (90 per cent) and Bulgaria (75 per cent), and Britain, with the USA, predominance in Greece (90 per cent). Yugoslavia and Hungary were shared 50/50.
notes.tip: Do not call the percentages agreement a treaty, and do not say Britain had a share of Yugoslavia: Greece was the British 90 per cent, while Yugoslavia and Hungary were 50/50.

notes.h: Yalta, February 1945
notes.b: Yalta was the last wartime meeting of the three leaders, held while Germany's defeat was certain. It settled how Germany would be handled and made promises about Poland, but it did not divide Europe.
points: The Yalta Conference met in the Crimea from 4 to 11 February 1945, attended by Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin.
Germany was to be divided into occupation zones, with France to receive one, and Berlin was to be divided into sectors. These arrangements fixed who would hold which part of Germany after surrender.
On Poland, the Soviet-backed Lublin government was to be broadened to include non-communists and free elections were promised. Poland's eastern border was also moved west.
The Declaration on Liberated Europe promised free elections in liberated states. Stalin's later disregard of it fed Western distrust, because the promise was broken in the very states it covered.
The Soviet Union agreed to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat, and a founding conference of the United Nations was agreed (held in San Francisco in April 1945).
Yalta is often blamed for splitting Europe, but it only agreed zones for Germany and promises on Poland. The division followed from the Red Army's presence on the ground and from later events.
notes.tip: Yalta (February 1945: Roosevelt, Churchill, Stalin) and Potsdam (July–August 1945: Truman, Stalin, Churchill then Attlee) are easily mixed up. Tie each to its leaders, and do not say Yalta 'divided Europe'.

notes.h: New leaders, the atomic bomb and Soviet security aims, 1945
notes.b: Between Yalta and the end of the war the people and the balance of power changed. New Western leaders, a new weapon and the Red Army's position in eastern Europe all hardened attitudes.
points: Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 and Harry Truman became president. Truman took a harder line towards Moscow, so cooperation became less likely.
Clement Attlee replaced Churchill as British prime minister in July 1945, during the Potsdam Conference, after a British election. Truman, Stalin and Attlee therefore finished the conference.
By May 1945 the Red Army held Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, eastern Germany and most of Czechoslovakia. Soviet power on the ground shaped what the West could demand.

Stalin, as reported by the Yugoslav communist Milovan Djilas, said that whoever occupies a territory also imposes on it his own social system. This shows what he expected to happen where the Red Army stood.

Stalin wanted a buffer zone (a belt of friendly states acting as a barrier) along his western frontier, and a sphere of influence in eastern Europe. He argued this was needed for security after the invasions of 1914 and 1941 and the losses of the war.
Historians ask how far these aims were defensive. Whatever Stalin's intention, Western leaders saw a buffer zone built by force and rigged politics as expansion.

The USA tested its first atomic bomb on 16 July 1945, during Potsdam, and used atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August). This gave the USA a monopoly, a weapon the Soviet Union lacked, until the first Soviet atomic test in August 1949.

notes.h: Potsdam: aims for Germany, July–August 1945
notes.b: At Potsdam the victors had to decide what to do with a defeated Germany. They agreed broad aims, but because each power ran its own zone, the aims were never fully put into practice.
points: The Potsdam Conference met from 17 July to 2 August 1945. Truman and Stalin were joined by Churchill, who was then replaced by Attlee.

Potsdam set four aims, the four Ds: demilitarisation, denazification, democratisation and decentralisation. Germany was also to be run as a single economic unit, so that the zones would not become separate economies.
On reparations (payment taken from a defeated state for war damage), each power took them from its own zone. The Soviet Union was also to get a share of industrial equipment from the western zones.
Land east of the Oder and Neisse rivers was placed under Polish administration until a peace treaty. Millions of Germans were expelled from it and from Czechoslovakia.

No peace treaty followed, so Germany remained under the four occupying powers, who met as the Allied Control Council in Berlin. It could act only if all four agreed, which made disagreement easy to turn into deadlock.
notes.tip: Do not write that the Soviets demanded reparations from the Ruhr and the West refused. At Potsdam the Soviets were given a share of western equipment, and the dispute came later, when the US zone stopped deliveries in 1946.

notes.h: Occupied Germany: the zones and Berlin
notes.b: Germany was run by four occupying powers, each controlling one area. Berlin, the old capital, was inside the Soviet zone, and that position later made it the focus of tension.
points: The Soviet Union held the east, Britain the north-west (including the Ruhr, the industrial heartland), and the USA the south. France held the south-west.
The zones were planned by the Allies in 1944, but France's zone was agreed at Yalta and carved out of the American and British zones. So France came in later and was the junior partner.
Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone. It was divided into four sectors: Soviet (east), American, British and French.

The Western sectors could be reached only along agreed routes through Soviet-held territory. This meant the Western powers depended on Soviet cooperation to supply their part of the city, and gave Stalin a way to apply pressure.
notes.tip: Exams on why Berlin became the focus of tension want you to explain cause, not narrate: stress Berlin's position deep inside the Soviet zone, with Western access only by agreed routes.

notes.h: The zones drift apart, 1945–1947
notes.b: The Allies had agreed to treat Germany as one unit, but the occupiers wanted different things. Between 1945 and 1947 the Soviet and Western zones moved steadily apart.
points: The Soviet Union dismantled factories and took reparations from its zone, which slowed recovery there. The West wanted German industry to revive, so the two policies pulled in opposite directions.
In 1946 General Lucius Clay, the US military governor, halted reparations deliveries from the US zone to the Soviet Union.

In September 1946 the US Secretary of State James Byrnes made a speech at Stuttgart saying the USA would stay in Germany and wanted its recovery. It told Germans and the Soviets that the West would not withdraw.

In April 1946 the Socialist Unity Party (SED) was formed in the Soviet zone by the forced merger of the communists and the social democrats. This gave the Soviet zone a ruling party under communist control.

On 1 January 1947 the American and British zones were merged as Bizonia, to make recovery easier. By 1947 the Western powers had concluded that the single economy agreed at Potsdam could not be restored.
notes.tip: Bizonia (January 1947) and Trizonia (1948–49, when the French zone joined) are different stages. Keep the dates apart.

notes.h: The open breach in 1946: Kennan, Stalin and the Iron Curtain
notes.b: In 1946 both sides stopped hiding their suspicions. Speeches and telegrams put into words the idea that the two systems were opponents.
points: In his election speech of February 1946, Stalin said capitalism made war inevitable. Western leaders took this as a sign that he saw conflict with them as unavoidable.

George Kennan, a US diplomat in Moscow, sent his Long Telegram on 22 February 1946. It argued that Soviet hostility was built into the Soviet system and that Soviet power would yield to firm resistance.
Containment, the American policy of resisting the spread of Soviet power and communism, was named in Kennan's anonymous 'X' article of 1947. The telegram supplied the ideas, not the word.
The Soviet counterpart was the Novikov telegram of September 1946, which described the USA as seeking world supremacy. The two sides were reading each other in the worst light.

Churchill spoke at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, with Truman present: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.' Stettin is now Szczecin in Poland.
The Iron Curtain was Churchill's image of the line dividing Soviet-controlled eastern Europe from the West. Later the term was used for the fortified border itself.
Stalin replied in Pravda in March 1946, comparing Churchill to Hitler and calling the speech a call to war against the Soviet Union.
notes.tip: The Long Telegram (February 1946), the Fulton speech (March 1946) and the 'X' article (1947) are easily mixed. Do not say the Long Telegram gave the word 'containment'.

notes.h: Greece, Turkey and the Truman Doctrine, 1947
notes.b: By 1947 Britain was too weak to keep supporting states on the edge of Soviet influence. The USA stepped in, and in doing so announced a principle that guided its policy for years.
points: In February 1947 Britain told the USA that it could no longer support Greece and Turkey, because it could not afford to. This created the opening for the USA to take on that role.

The Greek Civil War (1946–49) was fought between the government and communist guerrillas. The guerrillas were defeated in 1949 and Greece stayed in the Western camp; it was the first test of the Truman Doctrine.
Turkey was under Soviet pressure over the Straits (the waterway linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean), so it also looked to the West.
On 12 March 1947 Truman asked Congress for about 400 million dollars for Greece and Turkey. Congress approved it in May 1947.

Truman went wider than these two states: 'It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' This is the Truman Doctrine, a commitment to contain communism, not just to help Greece.
notes.tip: Truman Doctrine (March 1947: political and military aid to Greece and Turkey) and Marshall Plan (June 1947: economic aid open to all Europe) must be kept apart in answers.

notes.h: The Marshall Plan
notes.b: Truman's doctrine offered help to states under direct pressure. The Marshall Plan offered economic help to the whole of Europe, on the reasoning that hunger and ruin would make communism attractive.
points: George Marshall, the US Secretary of State, announced the plan in a speech at Harvard University on 5 June 1947.
Its aims were economic recovery, stopping communism's appeal (people who are poor and desperate are more likely to turn to communists), and rebuilding European markets for American goods.
The European Recovery Programme ran from 1948 to 1952 and provided about 13 billion dollars, mostly as grants. Ireland took part, receiving its aid mostly as loans.
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in April 1948, with 16 states sharing the aid and coordinating how it was used.
The offer was open to all of Europe, but Stalin forbade eastern states to take part. The aid therefore helped Western Europe recover while deepening the division of the continent.
notes.tip: A Marshall Aid answer needs who announced it, when and where, the amount (about), mostly grants, the ERP and OEEC, the aim of containing communism, and why the Soviet bloc refused. Say what it did for the Cold War division as well as for recovery.

notes.h: The Soviet response: Cominform, the Molotov Plan and Comecon
notes.b: Stalin saw Marshall aid as a way of drawing eastern Europe into the Western camp. He answered by tightening control over his allies and tying their economies to Moscow.
points: The Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov left the Paris talks on the plan in July 1947. Czechoslovakia and Poland had wanted to attend, but withdrew under Soviet pressure in the same month.
The 'Molotov Plan' was a name for the bilateral trade agreements that bound eastern Europe to Moscow from 1947. It was not a formal aid programme like Marshall's, so give it no figure.
The Cominform (Communist Information Bureau) was founded in September 1947 at a meeting in Poland, linking nine communist parties, including the French and Italian, under Soviet direction.

At the meeting Andrei Zhdanov gave his 'two camps' speech: the world was divided into an imperialist camp led by the USA and a democratic camp led by the Soviet Union. This left no room for neutrality.
The Comintern (Communist International) had been dissolved in 1943. The Cominform was a different body, made up of parties and aimed at keeping them in line.
Comecon, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, was set up in January 1949 as the bloc's economic answer to the Marshall Plan.
notes.tip: Comintern (dissolved 1943), Cominform (1947, parties) and Comecon (1949, economies) are a common muddle. Learn one fact for each.

notes.h: Sovietisation: stages and methods
notes.b: Sovietisation was the remaking of eastern European states on the Soviet model: one-party communist rule, secret police, a planned economy, collectivised farming and loyalty to Moscow, imposed with Red Army backing. It happened in stages and by a set of repeated methods.
points: The historian Hugh Seton-Watson (The East European Revolution, 1950) described three stages: genuine coalition, bogus coalition and monolithic (single-party) regime. The takeovers were complete by 1948.

In the first stage, communist parties governed through coalitions with peasant, socialist and liberal parties while taking key posts, such as the interior ministry (which controlled the police), for themselves.
Salami tactics means removing opponents one slice at a time, so that no single step provoked a united resistance. The phrase is usually attributed to the Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi.

The tools were the Red Army's presence, Soviet and local secret police, communist control of interior ministries and police, and land reform to win over peasants. They also included rigged elections, arrests and show trials, and forced mergers of socialist parties into communist ones.
Land reform in 1945–47 broke up large estates in Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and the Soviet zone of Germany and gave land to small farmers, which helped the communists win support.
A satellite state is formally independent but controlled by the Soviet Union in politics, economy and defence. By 1948 the states of eastern Europe had become satellites.
notes.tip: Marks go for method shown with a named country, a named victim and a date for each. Cover at least four countries, not just Czechoslovakia.

notes.h: Sovietisation in Poland and Hungary
notes.b: Poland, where the Soviet Union had the strongest interest, and Hungary, where the communists began weak, show how the same methods worked in different conditions.
points: Poland: the Soviet Union backed the communist-dominated Lublin government (formed in 1944), while Britain and the USA backed the London government-in-exile. Poland was the first flashpoint.
Poland: leaders of the Polish underground were arrested in 1945 and tried in Moscow in June 1945 (the Trial of the Sixteen), which removed non-communist resistance leaders early.
Poland: the election of January 1947 was rigged, and the Peasant Party leader and deputy prime minister Stanisław Mikołajczyk fled in October 1947.

Poland: the Polish Workers' Party and the Polish Socialist Party merged into the Polish United Workers' Party (PZPR) in December 1948, ending independent socialist opposition. Bolesław Bierut became the leading communist, as president.
Poland: Władysław Gomułka was removed as party leader in 1948 for 'nationalist deviation' and later arrested, showing that even communists who sought a separate path were purged.
Hungary: in the free election of November 1945 the Smallholders won about 57 per cent and the communists only about 17 per cent. The communists therefore had to use police power rather than votes.

Hungary: Rákosi used the police and interior ministry to break the Smallholders. Their leader Béla Kovács was arrested by Soviet forces in February 1947 and Prime Minister Ferenc Nagy was forced to resign in May 1947.

Hungary: the August 1947 election was rigged and the communists became the largest party with about 22 per cent. Communists and social democrats merged in June 1948; the Hungarian People's Republic followed in 1949.
notes.tip: Do not call Hungary's 1945 election rigged: it was free and the communists lost. The rigging came in 1947. Do not confuse Ferenc Nagy (forced out in 1947) with Imre Nagy of 1956.

notes.h: Sovietisation in Romania, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia, and the Church and Rajk in Hungary
notes.b: In the rest of the region the pattern was the same: pressure from the Red Army and the police, then the removal of the leading opponent.
points: Hungary: Cardinal József Mindszenty was arrested in December 1948, tried in February 1949 and given life imprisonment. This showed that the Church, a source of opposition, was also under attack.

Hungary: László Rajk, a communist who had been interior minister (running the police) and then foreign minister, was tried in September 1949 and executed in October 1949, so even leading communists were show-trial victims.
Romania: the Groza government was imposed under Soviet pressure in March 1945. The National Peasant leader Iuliu Maniu was tried in 1947 and imprisoned for life.
Romania: King Michael was forced to abdicate on 30 December 1947 and a people's republic was proclaimed.
Bulgaria: the Fatherland Front was a communist-dominated coalition. The monarchy was abolished after a referendum in September 1946 and Georgi Dimitrov became communist prime minister.
Bulgaria: the Agrarian leader Nikola Petkov was hanged in September 1947, which removed the main opposition leader.

Czechoslovakia: in the May 1946 election the communists were the largest party with about 38 per cent, and Klement Gottwald became prime minister. It was the only eastern state to stay democratic until 1948.

Czechoslovakia: on 20 February 1948 non-communist ministers resigned over communist control of the police. President Edvard Beneš accepted a communist-dominated government on 25 February, and he resigned in June 1948.
notes.tip: Don't say the Czechoslovak communists seized power by armed coup: it was a constitutional crisis exploited with police, militia and mass pressure, and Beneš accepted the new government. Don't say Jan Masaryk was murdered or killed himself, because the cause is disputed.

notes.h: Masaryk's death, the Soviet zone of Germany, Yugoslavia and Albania
notes.b: Two stories fit awkwardly into the pattern: the Soviet zone of Germany, which became a state of its own, and Yugoslavia and Albania, which had communist governments that did not depend on the Red Army.
points: Jan Masaryk, the non-communist foreign minister, was found dead below his window on 10 March 1948. Whether it was murder or suicide is still disputed, but it shocked Western opinion. He was the son of Tomáš Masaryk, Czechoslovakia's founding president.
In the Soviet zone of Germany the SED, formed in 1946, ruled alongside the dismantling of industry. Walter Ulbricht was the leading German communist, and the zone was on the road to becoming the GDR.
Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito and Albania under Enver Hoxha had communist governments that came to power largely through their own wartime resistance, not the Red Army. Tito was a partisan leader.

Because Tito did not owe his power to Moscow, he could resist Stalin. Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform in June 1948, showing that a communist state could break from Moscow without ceasing to be communist.

Purges of 'Titoists' followed elsewhere, including Rajk in Hungary, Traicho Kostov, a Bulgarian communist executed in December 1949, and Gomułka in Poland. Slánský in Czechoslovakia followed later, in 1952.

notes.h: Stalinisation after 1948 and why opposition failed
notes.b: After 1948 the satellites were made to copy the Soviet Union in detail. The forces that might have resisted had by then been broken one by one.
points: The Soviet model was copied: central planning, heavy industry, the start of collectivisation of farms, the cult of Stalin and further purges. This made the states satellites, not just friendly neighbours.

Opposition came from peasant parties, the Church, socialists and, in Poland, an armed underground. Each was dealt with separately, which is why salami tactics worked: no group could count on the others.
The peasant parties lost their leaders (Mikołajczyk, Kovács, Petkov, Maniu) and the socialists were merged into communist parties, such as the SED and the PZPR, so they lost their independence.
The Church was attacked, as Mindszenty's trial shows. The Red Army and secret police stood behind the local communists, so open resistance risked Soviet force.
Yugoslavia was the partial exception, because there was no Red Army occupation and Tito's own partisans held power.
notes.tip: On how successful opposition was, pair each opposition force with its fate and name Yugoslavia as the only real exception, with the reason: no Red Army occupation and Tito's own partisans.

notes.h: Towards a West German state: the London talks and the currency reform
notes.b: As Soviet and Western policies on Germany diverged, the Western powers decided to build a West German state and to revive its economy. The currency reform was the step that brought the crisis.
points: The London Six-Power Conference (USA, Britain, France and the Benelux countries) met from February to June 1948 and recommended a West German state. This broke with the idea of treating Germany as a single unit.
In March 1948 the Soviet delegate walked out of the Allied Control Council, ending four-power government of Germany.
The French zone joined the Bizone in 1948–49 (Trizonia), creating a single western area.
On 20 June 1948 a currency reform in the western zones introduced the Deutsche Mark, and it was extended to West Berlin.
Moscow saw the reform as a threat because it signalled a lasting West German state.

notes.h: The Berlin Blockade and airlift, 1948–1949
notes.b: Stalin used Berlin's position inside the Soviet zone to try to reverse Western plans. The Western reply was to supply the city by air, which turned a Soviet pressure tactic into a Western propaganda success.
points: The Soviet Union blockaded road, rail and canal links to West Berlin, and the blockade was complete from 24 June 1948. West Berlin had a population of over 2 million.
Stalin's aims were to make the West drop the new currency and the West German state, or leave Berlin altogether.
The Western powers organised an airlift from June 1948 to September 1949, called Operation Vittles by the Americans and Operation Plainfare by the British.
Planes used three airfields: Tempelhof (American sector), Gatow (British) and Tegel (French, built during the airlift). At its peak about one plane landed a minute.
About 2.3 million tons of supplies were delivered. Truman refused to withdraw.

General Lucius Clay, the US military governor, and Ernst Reuter led the Western and Berlin response. Reuter led West Berlin and became its mayor in December 1948, and in September 1948 he appealed to the people of the world to look upon the city.
The blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949, though the airlift continued until September 1949.
notes.tip: A Berlin Blockade answer needs cause (currency reform, West German state plans), events (what was cut, the airlift, the airfields, Clay and Reuter), the end in May 1949 and the results. Do not describe Reuter as simply the mayor throughout, and do not give casualty or flight numbers.

notes.h: The results: two German states
notes.b: The blockade failed, and by the end of 1949 Germany had two states. Berlin became a symbol and a flashpoint, and the crisis pushed the West towards a military alliance.
points: The blockade was a Western propaganda victory: the West was seen as feeding a city that the Soviet Union tried to starve. It confirmed Germany's division and pushed the West towards NATO.
The Federal Republic of Germany was founded on 23 May 1949 under a Basic Law, with Bonn as its capital. Konrad Adenauer, a Christian Democrat, became chancellor in September 1949.

The German Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 7 October 1949 in the Soviet zone. Wilhelm Pieck was president and Otto Grotewohl prime minister, but Walter Ulbricht was the leading figure in the SED.
East Berlin was the capital of the GDR, while West Berlin was run by the Western powers and closely tied to the Federal Republic, so Berlin stayed divided.
notes.tip: Keep the dates in order: blockade lifted (12 May 1949), FRG founded (23 May 1949), airlift ended (September 1949), Adenauer chancellor (September 1949), GDR (7 October 1949). The Berlin Blockade of 1948–49 is not the Berlin Wall of 1961.

notes.h: Military alliances: Brussels Treaty, NATO and the Warsaw Pact
notes.b: Fear of Soviet power led the Western states to ally, and later the Soviet Union created a rival alliance. The two alliances made the division of Europe a military one as well as a political and economic one.
points: The Brussels Treaty of 17 March 1948 linked Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. It was the starting point for NATO.

The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve states: the USA, Canada, Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Portugal and Italy.
Article 5 says that an attack on one member is an attack on all. This tied US troops to Europe, so the USA was committed to defend it.
Lord Ismay, NATO's first Secretary General (1952), is credited with saying its purpose was 'to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.' Greece and Turkey joined in 1952.
West Germany joined NATO in May 1955, after its rearmament was agreed; the European Defence Community had failed in 1954.

The Warsaw Pact was signed in Warsaw on 14 May 1955, as the Soviet reply to West German entry into NATO. Its members were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, East Germany and Albania, with a Soviet commander and Soviet troops in member states.
Albania stopped taking part in the early 1960s and formally left in 1968.
notes.tip: Give the dates in the right order: Brussels Treaty (1948), NATO (1949), West Germany's entry (May 1955), then the Warsaw Pact (14 May 1955). Do not mix up the Brussels Treaty (five states) with NATO (twelve).

notes.h: Assessment: who caused the Cold War?
notes.b: Historians disagree about who was to blame, and the opening of Soviet archives after 1991 changed the terms of the debate. Good answers pair the views and finish with a judgement.
points: Orthodox view: Western writers of the 1940s and 1950s blamed Stalin's drive to expand and the threat it posed to Western Europe. Evidence for this is the way eastern Europe was taken over by rigged elections, purges and one-party rule.
Revisionist view: William Appleman Williams, in The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959), argued that US economic expansion and the atomic monopoly provoked Soviet hostility.

Post-revisionist view: mutual misperception, each side reading the other's defensive moves as threats. John Lewis Gaddis later, after the archives partly opened, put more weight on Stalin in We Now Know (1997).

Stalin's control of eastern Europe went far beyond a defensive buffer. Historians who stress the defensive side point to the wartime invasions of Russia and the huge war losses; those who stress the offensive side point to the speed with which communist rule was imposed in 1947–48.
Western decisions such as the currency reform of June 1948 deepened the division of Germany, which Soviet leaders could regard as a threat; so each side's actions made the other's worse.
notes.tip: Top answers on the origins of the Cold War show how each step made the next worse, from wartime distrust through Yalta, Potsdam, the bomb, Fulton, the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, Cominform, Czechoslovakia and Berlin to NATO and the two German states, and end with a judgement on blame.

notes.h: Assessment: how successful was Soviet control of Eastern Europe by 1949?
notes.b: By 1949 Stalin had built a bloc of communist states, but the bloc had limits and had provoked a strong Western reaction.
points: Achievement: eight communist states were under Soviet leadership, with one-party rule in each by 1948.
Achievement: the Cominform tied the parties to Moscow and Comecon tied the economies, so the bloc had political and economic institutions of its own.
Achievement: purges of rivals, including Rajk and Kostov, kept the local communist leaders obedient.
Limit: Tito's Yugoslavia broke away in 1948 and survived, so Soviet control was not complete.
Limit: the West held Berlin through the airlift, so the Soviet attempt to push the West out failed.

Limit: Marshall aid revived Western Europe and the Soviet bloc could not match it, and NATO (1949) united the West against Soviet pressure. Stalin's actions had therefore strengthened the West he feared.
notes.tip: For how successful Soviet control was, set achievements (one-party states, Cominform, Comecon, purges of Titoists) against limits (Tito, failure in Berlin, the West's recovery and NATO).

keyTerms.definition: The rivalry from 1945 to 1991 between the USA and its allies and the Soviet Union and its eastern European bloc, short of direct war between them.
Churchill's term for the division of Europe between the Soviet-controlled east and the democracies of the west, and the physical border that later enclosed the Soviet bloc.
The process by which communist parties backed by the Soviet Union took control of eastern European states and remodelled their politics, economies and police on the Soviet pattern.
A state formally independent but dominated politically and militarily by the Soviet Union, as the eastern European states were after 1945.
An economic system in which private owners run businesses for profit in competitive markets, which the Western powers defended against communism.
A political and economic system in which a single communist party directs the state and the economy is publicly owned and centrally planned.
The 1947 US policy of giving economic and military aid to countries threatened by communism, beginning with Greece and Turkey.
The Communist Information Bureau founded in 1947 to coordinate the European communist parties under Soviet direction.
The Soviet cut-off of land access to West Berlin from June 1948 to May 1949, which the Western powers countered with an airlift.
The step-by-step removal of non-communist rivals, slice by slice, by which communists took power in eastern Europe; usually attributed to Mátyás Rákosi.
The American programme of economic aid to Western Europe (the European Recovery Programme, 1948–52), offered in June 1947 to rebuild economies and weaken the appeal of communism.
The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, set up in 1949 to coordinate trade and economic planning among the Soviet bloc states.

factCards.term: Yalta, February 1945: what was agreed on Germany
factCards.definition: Germany was to be divided into occupation zones run by the USA, Britain, France and the Soviet Union, with Berlin split into four sectors.

factCards.term: Fulton, March 1946: the speech and its wording
factCards.definition: Churchill said an iron curtain had descended from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic, speaking at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri.
Truman asked Congress in March 1947 for about 400 million dollars of aid for Greece and Turkey; Congress approved it in May 1947.

factCards.term: Marshall Plan: the year and the sum
factCards.definition: Announced in June 1947 at Harvard, the aid package of about 13 billion dollars ran through the European Recovery Programme from 1948 to 1952.

factCards.term: Salami tactics: who is credited with the phrase
factCards.definition: Mátyás Rákosi, the Hungarian communist leader, is usually credited with the phrase for removing rivals one thin slice at a time.
Non-communist ministers resigned over control of the police, and Klement Gottwald's communists took power without an election.
King Michael was forced to abdicate on 30 December 1947 and a people's republic was declared.
Yugoslavia was expelled in June 1948, showing that a communist state could defy Moscow and survive.

factCards.term: Berlin airlift: the end of the blockade
factCards.definition: The Soviet blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949 after the Western airlift had kept West Berlin supplied for about eleven months.
The Federal Republic of Germany was founded on 23 May 1949 under a Basic Law, with Konrad Adenauer as chancellor from September 1949.
The German Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 7 October 1949 in the Soviet zone.
Signed in Warsaw on 14 May 1955 by the Soviet Union and seven eastern European states, a response to West German entry into NATO.

factCards.term: Kennan's Long Telegram: date and idea
factCards.definition: Sent on 22 February 1946, it argued that Soviet expansion should be contained by firm resistance at points of pressure.

factCards.term: Czechoslovakia: the death of Jan Masaryk
factCards.definition: The non-communist foreign minister died in a fall from a window on 10 March 1948, shortly after the communist takeover; the cause remains disputed.
Demilitarisation, denazification, democratisation and decentralisation, with the economy treated as a single unit.
